title: Pyrography animal scene on a spoon
subtitle: Pyrography: burning an animal silhouette or scene onto the back of a carved spoon
excerpt: Burning an animal scene onto the back of a carved wooden spoon, a fox, hare, or bird in a simple composition on the convex surface. The curved surface of a spoon back changes how the pen sits compared to a flat panel; this guide covers adapting the technique for working on a curved form, and choosing subjects that suit the small available area.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Book of Drawing and Design (1899) for the silhouette composition on curved surfaces.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of burning designs into wood using a heated metal tip.
Small wooden household objects, spoons, bowls, cups, made by hand carving rather than turning. From the Old English word for tree.

content.text: Burning a design onto a spoon back turns a functional piece of
treen
into a decorative one. The spoon back is the right surface for
pyrography

because it is convex and presents naturally to view when the spoon is displayed. A simple animal silhouette, fox, hare, wren, robin, in a seated or running pose fits the teardrop shape of the spoon back and reads clearly at small scale.
Before you start burning.
Ventilation: pyrography produces wood smoke. Work near an open window or use a fume extractor. Do not burn in an enclosed room.
Hot tip: the pyrography tip reaches 200, 400 °C. Never touch it. Set the pen on its stand when not burning.
Fire: keep the pen unit away from flammable materials. Do not leave unattended when on.
First aid: contact burn, cool water for 20 minutes. A&E if larger than a 5p coin.
What you need

A carved spoon, fully finished and sanded to 240 grit, not yet oiled. Pyrography should be done before the final oil finish, oil darkens the wood and makes it harder to see the burn marks. The spoon wood should be lime, sycamore, cherry, or birch, not oak (the hard rings create uneven burning on a curved surface) and not softwood (too fast-burning and uneven).
Choosing and fitting the design

The spoon back area for burning is typically 4, 6 cm by 3, 4 cm, a small area. Choose a design that reads as a silhouette: the animal outline should be recognisable without internal detail. A seated hare fits the roughly oval spoon back well. Draw the design to size on paper first and hold it against the spoon back to check scale.
Transferring to a curved surface

Carbon transfer paper does not sit flat on a curved surface. Instead, draw the design directly onto the spoon back with a soft pencil, using the paper drawing as a reference. The pencil line will be covered by the burn; it is only needed to guide the pen. Alternatively, cut the transfer paper into a series of small triangular segments that can be laid flat on the curved surface individually.
Burning on a curved surface

The main challenge is that the pen angle relative to the wood surface changes as the pen follows the curve of the spoon back. At the edges of the spoon back, the pen tip is at a more acute angle than at the centre. The solution is to rotate the spoon rather than tilting the pen: keep the pen at a constant angle and rotate the spoon so the burning surface is always at the same angle to the pen. Work across the back of the spoon by rotating it continuously toward you as you burn.
Finishing the decorated spoon

After burning, apply raw linseed oil for a food-use spoon, or beeswax for a display spoon. Both finishes deepen the contrast between the pale wood and the burn. For a food-use spoon with a burn decoration, keep the burn away from the bowl, the bowl area contacts food and can harbour carbon residue in scratched burn marks. The back and handle are the right surfaces for pyrography on functional spoons.

attrs.symptom: The burn marks on the spoon back are much darker at the edges than the centre
attrs.cause: The pen is staying at a fixed angle while the surface curves away, creating a more acute contact angle at the edges which burns more slowly and darkly
attrs.fix: Rotate the spoon so the burning area is always parallel to the pen. At the spoon edge, tilt the spoon toward you to bring the surface back to 90 degrees to the pen tip.
